questions.explanation: reduce folds every element into the accumulator starting from zero, producing the sum 917. The initial value is the seed, not an extra element. The printed value is 917, while the alternatives come from taking only the first element, omitting the last element and starting the accumulator at one.
questions.hint: The accumulator starts at the supplied initial value.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving strings — charat.

options.misconception: Reading index zero instead of one

questions.explanation: charAt returns the character at the given zero-based index; index 1 of '895' is '9'. Index zero would be the first digit, not the second. The printed value is 9, while the alternatives come from reading index zero instead of one, reading the final digit and choosing the next digit instead.
questions.hint: String positions start counting at zero.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving strings — slice.

stimulus.body: A program is processing the value 896.

options.misconception: Assuming slice copies the whole string

questions.explanation: With one argument, slice returns everything from that index to the end, dropping the first character of '896'. The result is '96'. The printed value is 96, while the alternatives come from assuming slice copies the whole string, keeping the removed first character and stopping after one character.
questions.hint: A single slice index means from there to the end.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving strings — split join.

options.misconception: Counting a separator after the last digit
Dropping a digit from the count

questions.explanation: split turns '897' into 3 characters and join inserts a dash between each pair, giving 5 characters. There are one fewer separators than digits. The printed value is 5, while the alternatives come from ignoring the inserted separators, counting a separator after the last digit and dropping a digit from the count.
questions.hint: Count the dashes between digits, not after the last one.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — access.
questions.explanation: Bracket access with the exact key string retrieves 898, and adding one gives 899. A mistyped key would produce undefined, not zero. Carrying the operation through gives 899; common slips include forgetting the addition of one and adding two by mistake.
questions.hint: Bracket notation uses the key name as a string.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — keys.

answer.exemplar: Object.keys returns the enumerable own property names, which are a, b and c, so its length is three. Values such as 899 do not affect the count. The result is 3.
